claims.text: An initially single-phase high-entropy alloy undergoes stress-assisted microsegregation under combined high-temperature and cyclic loading.
Stress-assisted microsegregation locally promotes nano-scale brittle precipitates at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary nano-precipitates trigger a transition from ductile to brittle fracture.
The as-cast initial alloy is uniformly mixed and single-phase.
The initial alloy has minimal grain-boundary segregation.
The initial alloy contains no secondary-phase precipitates.
Elevated temperature and cyclic loading accelerate atomic diffusion and stress-driven segregation.
Thermal activation and cyclic stress enhance the mobility of minor constituents.
Enhanced constituent mobility produces nonuniform partitioning at grain boundaries.
Local grain-boundary enrichment promotes nucleation of brittle nano-scale precipitates.
The precipitates undermine grain-boundary cohesion and thereby reduce toughness.
Samples exposed to combined high-temperature ageing and cyclic loading will exhibit lower toughness than the baseline.
Exposed samples will shift from ductile toward brittle fracture characteristics.
Microscopy or atom-probe analysis will reveal nano-scale grain-boundary precipitates after exposure that are absent from the as-cast baseline.
The initial baseline alloy has high toughness and ductile fracture behavior.
The proposed mechanism dominates only under sustained high-temperature and cyclic-loading service conditions.
Under lower-temperature or static-loading conditions, the alloy retains its homogeneous microstructure and toughness.
The temperature and stress thresholds for significant microsegregation and precipitation may depend on subtle compositional variations.
